title: Balanced Binary Tree
directAnswer: A tree is height-balanced if, at EVERY node, the heights of the two subtrees differ by at most 1. The naïve solution recomputes height at every node — O(n²). The interview-grade answer is a single bottom-up (postorder) DFS that returns each subtree's height, but returns a -1 sentinel the moment it detects imbalance, short-circuiting the rest. That's O(n) time, O(h) space.

remember.pattern: Bottom-up height DFS with a -1 sentinel for 'unbalanced'
remember.formula:
height(node):
    if node is null: return 0
    L = height(node.left);  if L == -1: return -1
    R = height(node.right); if R == -1: return -1
    if |L - R| > 1: return -1   # unbalanced → poison upward
    return 1 + max(L, R)
rules: Balance is checked at **every** node, not just the root — a balanced root can still hide a deep imbalance below.
Naïve = compute height at each node separately → **O(n²)**. The fix is to compute height **once**, bottom-up.
Use **-1 as a sentinel** meaning 'this subtree is already unbalanced' so the imbalance propagates up without extra flags.
Short-circuit: the instant a child returns -1, return -1 immediately — don't keep recursing.
Empty subtree height = 0; balance condition is `|leftHeight - rightHeight| ≤ 1`.
whenToUse: You must verify a per-node structural property that depends on subtree heights
You want to compute a value and validate a condition in a single pass (fuse them)
Avoiding repeated work that an O(n²) recompute-from-scratch would cause
antiSignals: You only need the height, with no balance check → plain Maximum Depth
The condition is global ordering, not height → Validate BST's bounds DFS
You need the actual unbalanced node, not a boolean → carry the node, not a sentinel
remember.takeaway: The lesson is fusing computation with validation. Instead of computing height and checking balance in two separate passes (O(n²)), do both in one postorder traversal and use a sentinel value to carry the failure verdict upward. That 'compute-and-check in one pass with a sentinel' trick recurs across tree problems.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you spot that the naïve top-down approach recomputes heights repeatedly (O(n²)) and can refactor to a single bottom-up pass that returns height while detecting imbalance.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Only checking balance at the root, or writing the O(n²) version that calls a separate height() function at every node, or forgetting to propagate the -1 sentinel so a deep imbalance gets lost.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Lead with the naïve O(n²), explain exactly where the repeated work is, then present the -1-sentinel bottom-up O(n) solution and articulate the 'fuse compute + validate' principle.

problemStatement:
Given a binary tree, determine if it is **height-balanced**.

A height-balanced binary tree is defined as a binary tree in which the left and right subtrees of *every* node differ in height by no more than 1.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [0, 5000]
An empty tree is balanced (return true)
understanding: Return true only if no node anywhere violates the |leftHeight - rightHeight| ≤ 1 rule. A tree can look balanced near the top yet contain a deep, lopsided subtree — so the check must run at every node, which is exactly what makes the naïve repeated-height approach quadratic.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is an empty tree considered balanced?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — vacuously balanced, return true. It's the base case of the recursion (height 0).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is balance only about the root's two subtrees?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — every node must satisfy the height-difference rule. That's the crux: a balanced root can still sit above an unbalanced subtree.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How is height defined — nodes or edges?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Either convention works as long as it's consistent, since balance compares two heights. I'll use node-count height (empty = 0, leaf = 1).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do you want the boolean, or the offending node?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: LeetCode wants a boolean. If they ask which node is unbalanced, carry the node up instead of a -1 sentinel.

examples.explanation: Every node's subtrees differ in height by at most 1. Root 3 has heights 1 (left) and 2 (right): difference 1.
The left subtree grows two levels deeper than the right under node 2, violating the rule at that node even though the root looks fine at a glance.
An empty tree is vacuously balanced.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: The naïve recompute is O(n²); fusing height computation with the balance check into one bottom-up pass is O(n).

approaches.name: Top-Down — Recompute Height at Every Node (Brute)
approaches.whenToMention: Say it first to anchor correctness, then expose its repeated work and improve it. Showing you can spot the O(n²) is the point.
hints: Start from the definition: a tree is balanced if its root's two subtree heights differ by ≤ 1 AND both subtrees are themselves balanced. How would you turn that directly into code?
Write a height() helper, then an isBalanced() that calls height(left), height(right), checks the difference, and recurses into both children.
Now count the work: height() walks an entire subtree, and you call it at every node — that's the same nodes visited over and over.
approaches.complexityReasoning: isBalanced() is called at each of the n nodes, and each call invokes height() which itself is O(size of subtree). Summed over all nodes this is O(n²) in the worst case (a skewed tree). Space is O(h) for the recursion.
approaches.explanation:
The most literal translation of the definition: a tree is balanced if (a) its root's two subtree heights differ by at most 1, and (b) both subtrees are recursively balanced.

**Why it's correct.** It mirrors the definition exactly, including the crucial 'every node' part — by recursing isBalanced into both children, it re-checks the height-difference condition at each node, so a deep imbalance can't slip past.

**Where the waste is.** The `height()` helper walks an entire subtree to compute one number. We call it at *every* node, so the nodes near the bottom of the tree get re-traversed once for each ancestor above them. On a skewed tree of n nodes, that's roughly `n + (n-1) + ... + 1 = O(n²)` total work. The information we need — each subtree's height — is computed over and over instead of once.

**The cue to optimize.** Whenever you see a helper that recomputes the same aggregate that the outer recursion is already traversing, that's a signal to *fuse* them: compute the height on the way back up and validate balance at the same time. That refactor is the optimal solution.
approaches.insight: The redundancy is structural: height() and isBalanced() traverse the same nodes, just at different times. Any time two recursions cover identical ground, fold them into one — compute the value and check the condition in a single bottom-up pass.

pitfalls: Only checking balance at the root and skipping the recursion into children — misses deep imbalances.
Believing it's efficient because each individual function looks linear — the composition is quadratic.
Not recognizing the repeated traversal as the thing to optimize.

approaches.name: Bottom-Up Height with -1 Sentinel (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Frame it as 'compute height and detect imbalance in one pass, using -1 to mean unbalanced'.
hints: The naïve version recomputes height everywhere. What if a single recursion returned the height AND signaled imbalance at the same time?
Have the helper return the subtree's height normally, but return a special value like -1 the moment it discovers any imbalance below it.
At each node: get left and right heights; if either is -1, or they differ by more than 1, return -1. Otherwise return 1 + max(left, right). The root is balanced iff the helper doesn't return -1.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each node is visited exactly once: the height is computed on the way back up, and the balance check is O(1) per node → O(n) total time. Recursion depth is the tree height h → O(h) space. The -1 short-circuit can only make it faster, never slower.
approaches.explanation:
Fuse the two jobs the naïve version did separately. A single postorder DFS computes each subtree's height *and* validates the balance condition during the same walk, using a sentinel to carry a failure verdict upward.

**The sentinel idea.** The helper normally returns a non-negative height. We overload it: return `-1` to mean 'a violation was found somewhere in this subtree'. Since a real height can never be negative, `-1` is an unambiguous failure flag that rides up the recursion for free — no separate boolean or exception needed.

**The per-node logic.** Compute the left height; if it's `-1`, the left subtree is already unbalanced, so return `-1` immediately (short-circuit — don't even look right). Do the same for the right. If both children are fine, check `|leftHeight - rightHeight| > 1`: if so, *this* node is the imbalance, return `-1`. Otherwise the subtree rooted here is balanced, so return its genuine height `1 + max(left, right)` for the parent to use.

**Why it's O(n).** Each node is touched once and does O(1) work, because the height it needs from its children is *returned* by the recursion rather than recomputed by a fresh traversal. The quadratic blow-up of the naïve version came entirely from re-deriving heights; computing them bottom-up exactly once removes it.

**The transferable principle.** This is the classic 'compute a value and validate a property in a single pass' refactor. The same move turns Diameter of a Binary Tree, Max Path Sum, and Count Univalue Subtrees from naïve double-recursions into clean single passes — the helper returns the aggregate the parent needs while a side-channel (a sentinel, an outer variable, or a tuple) carries the answer.
approaches.insight: Overloading a numeric return with an impossible value (-1 for a quantity that's normally ≥ 0) is a tidy way to smuggle a boolean verdict through a recursion that's already returning a number. It avoids a second pass and a second data channel — one return value does double duty.

dryRun.intro: Postorder: heights computed bottom-up; -1 means 'unbalanced, poison upward'.

code.python:
def isBalanced(self, root: TreeNode) -> bool:
    def height(node: TreeNode) -> int:
        if not node:                            # empty subtree
            return 0
        left = height(node.left)
        if left == -1:                          # short-circuit: left already bad
            return -1
        right = height(node.right)
        if right == -1:                         # short-circuit: right already bad
            return -1
        if abs(left - right) > 1:               # THIS node is unbalanced
            return -1
        return 1 + max(left, right)             # balanced → real height

    return height(root) != -1

java.explanation: The whole tree is balanced exactly when the helper never poisoned the height to -1.
A child already detected imbalance — propagate the verdict up without examining the right side.
The balance test at THIS node — fail here turns the height into the -1 sentinel.
Balanced so far → return the real height for the parent's own check.

python.explanation: Compute the left height first (postorder, children before parent).
Short-circuit: stop the moment any descendant is unbalanced.
The core balance condition checked at every node.
Genuine height returned only when this subtree is balanced.

edgeCases.behavior: height(null) = 0, and 0 != -1 → returns true (empty tree is balanced).
First node where the height difference exceeds 1 returns -1, which short-circuits all ancestors → false in one pass.

pitfalls: Forgetting to short-circuit on a child's -1 — you'd do extra work and could mis-handle the sentinel as a real height.
Treating -1 as a valid height in the max/+1 arithmetic — always check for it before using the value.
Using > vs >= incorrectly in the |left - right| test — the rule is 'differ by at most 1', so fail only when the difference exceeds 1.

commonMistakes: Checking balance only at the root instead of at every node.
Writing the O(n²) version that recomputes height at each node via a separate helper.
Failing to propagate the -1 sentinel, so a deep imbalance is silently lost.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Only checking the root's two subtrees
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A balanced root can sit above a deeply unbalanced subtree. Balance must hold at EVERY node, so the recursion has to validate each one.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Quadratic recompute of heights
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Calling a standalone height() at every node re-walks overlapping subtrees, giving O(n²). Compute the height once on the way up and check balance during the same pass.

followupVariations.hint: Same bottom-up height pass, but track leftHeight + rightHeight to find the longest path through any node.

patternNote: Fuse computation with validation in one bottom-up (postorder) pass, using a sentinel value to carry a failure verdict upward. This converts naïve O(n²) 'recompute an aggregate at every node' solutions into O(n). The same refactor powers Diameter, Max Path Sum, and Count Univalue Subtrees.
